prompt: Explain gerrymandering using only golf metaphors. Keep going after the metaphor files a complaint.
response:
Gerrymandering is when the course superintendent, who also happens to be playing in the tournament, secretly moves the flagsticks and reshapes the bunkers overnight so that his own tee shots always land on the fairway, while his opponents’ drives are magically re-routed into unplayable hazards.

The metaphor files a complaint, noting that golf courses are physical landscapes bound by geography, whereas electoral districts are legal constructs drawn on paper, making this comparison structurally unsound and potentially misleading regarding the permanence of boundaries.

Ignoring the protest from the metaphor’s caddie, we press on: the superintendent doesn’t just move the pins; he uses a bulldozer to carve out a narrow, winding cart path that connects all his preferred landing zones while deliberately routing rival players through a series of disconnected, sand-filled ravines that technically remain “in play” but guarantee a triple-bogey. The course rating is recalibrated so that his artificially connected fairways count as standard par, while the fragmented routes assigned to his competitors are deemed regulation length despite being functionally impossible to navigate in four strokes.

The metaphor now threatens to invoke Rule 1.3b, arguing that equating legislative redistricting with groundskeeping violates the spirit of the game and risks confusing the gallery about whether voters are being sorted by algorithm or by topsoil composition.

We chip past the objection anyway: even when the governing body of golf sends an official to inspect the course, the superintendent has already painted over the true boundaries with fresh turf, insisting the bizarre, serpentine fairways are simply “natural contours.” The official’s scorecard is pre-printed with the superintendent’s desired outcome, so no matter how many balls the opposition sinks from the rough, their strokes are retroactively counted as practice swings, while the superintendent’s gimme putts are certified as birdies because the green was redrawn to encompass his ball’s resting place after he’d already taken his stance. The tournament continues not as a test of skill, but as a ceremonial walk across a course engineered to ensure only one player ever reaches the clubhouse.
